planting.note: Scatter seed on bare, thin soil in fall so it can overwinter as a tiny rosette and bloom at the first warm spell; it needs open ground with little competing vegetation to germinate well.

directions: Tiny bluet is a diminutive winter annual that carpets thin-soiled dolomite and limestone glades of the Ozark Highlands with pale lavender-blue, four-petaled flowers in late winter and very early spring, often finishing bloom before taller glade perennials even break dormancy. Seed germinates with cooling fall temperatures, overwinters as a small basal rosette, and the plant completes its life cycle quickly once warmth returns, so it is best suited to open, gravelly, unmulched ground such as a glade garden, rock garden, or thin lawn area rather than a conventional border. It reseeds readily where soil stays exposed and uncompeted, making it a good companion for other spring glade ephemerals, but it will not persist in rich, mulched, or densely planted beds. No fertilizer or irrigation is needed once it is established in lean, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring onto lean, well-drained soil in full sun; seed benefits from a winter chill and plants typically bloom their second year, then persist by reseeding.

directions: Longflower beeblossom sends up tall, airy, reddish-tinged stems lined with slender white flowers that open in the evening and fade to pink by the next afternoon, drawing in night-flying moths across Ozark glade margins and dry limestone prairie openings from mid to late summer. It behaves as a short-lived perennial or biennial, often flowering heaviest in its second year before declining, but it maintains a presence in a planting by reseeding freely on open, disturbed, well-drained ground. Give it full sun and lean soil; in richer garden conditions it grows floppier and may need the support of neighboring grasses or perennials to stay upright. It needs no fertilizing and tolerates drought and heat with ease once its deep taproot is established.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall onto thin, rocky, calcareous soil in full sun, or set out spring plugs into lean ground with sharp drainage; this aster resents rich, moisture-retentive garden soil.

directions: Manyray aster is a woody-based perennial restricted to dolomite and limestone glades of the Ozark and Ouachita region, where it survives thin, droughty, rocky soil that keeps most competing vegetation at bay. Its common name comes from flower heads bearing an unusually high number of narrow violet-blue ray florets around a yellow disc, opening in late summer and fall when most other glade wildflowers have finished blooming. The hairy, gray-green foliage and low, spreading, somewhat shrubby habit reflect its adaptation to intense summer heat and reflected light off exposed rock, and it is best grown in a rock garden, glade restoration, or xeric native bed rather than amended border soil. It needs no irrigation once rooted in and should not be divided or overwatered, as excess moisture and rich soil quickly weaken the plant.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring into consistently moist, mineral-rich soil at the edge of a glade seep, pond margin, or rain garden; it spreads by shallow rhizomes once established in wet ground.

directions: Unlike most meadow beauties of the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains, this inland species occurs in the scattered seeps and perennially damp swales that cut through otherwise dry dolomite glades of the Ozark interior, where shallow groundwater keeps a narrow band of soil wet even through summer drought on the surrounding rock. It produces the same showy four-petaled, bright pink flowers with curved, bright yellow anthers typical of the genus, held above narrow, bristly-margined leaves on wiry stems through mid and late summer. Because it depends on steady moisture at its roots even while tolerating full, baking sun, it is best used along the damp edge of a rain garden or pond rather than in an average perennial bed, and spreading rhizomes will slowly fill in bare wet ground once settled. Divide congested clumps in spring if they outgrow their space.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into the leaf litter of an oak-hickory woodland floor or along a shaded bluff edge; seed needs winter cold to break dormancy and seedlings establish best with light shade.

directions: MacGregor's wildrye is a cool-season bunchgrass of rich oak-hickory woodland floors and dry bluff-top margins across the Ozark and Interior Highlands, only recently recognized as distinct from the more familiar Virginia wildrye it closely resembles. It greens up and flowers noticeably earlier in spring than its relatives, sending up slender, arching seed heads above a modest clump of narrow blue-green leaves before much of the woodland canopy has fully closed in. Use it in a shaded native grass planting, woodland restoration, or bluff-edge mix where it adds early-season texture and later provides seed for woodland birds; it tolerates the dry, leaf-littered, rocky soil typical of Ozark timbered slopes without supplemental watering once established. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to keep stands tidy.

planting.note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring into moist, fertile soil along a woodland streambank, swale, or rain garden edge in partial shade to full sun; established clumps tolerate brief flooding and periodic dry spells alike.

directions: Short's sedge forms upright, dense tufts of broad, bright green blades along the seasonally wet swales, spring branches, and streambanks that drain Ozark-Ouachita oak-hickory woodlands, where it helps stabilize soil on banks that alternate between standing water and dry summer baseflow. Clusters of small, bristly seed heads appear on separate stalks above the foliage in late spring, adding a soft textural accent without flopping over like some larger wetland sedges. It adapts readily to cultivated rain gardens and pond margins as long as soil stays reliably moist to occasionally wet, and it holds up to both the partial shade of a streamside woodland edge and more open sun near open water. Division of overgrown clumps in spring is the simplest way to propagate and keep stands vigorous.
